articles.title: US universities are failing to protect victims of sexual assault
articles.summary: The Cornell case shows how university bureaucracy discourages complaints and shields institutions.
articles.body:
Cornell University’s internal processes for responding to sexual assault reports failed “Jane Doe”. In 2024, the third-year student reported being sexually assaulted by seven men while incapacitated at a fraternity house . Cornell launched an investigation that would last months, but the process failed to deliver the accountability Jane Doe sought. She was left feeling unheard and unsafe, dropping out without completing her degree. No criminal charges were brought against the men she accused. She is now suing Cornell over its handling of her case. None of the administrators involved in those processes have been named. They have yet to face accountability.

Her experience reveals the ways in which confidential procedures at universities are intended to make “problems” go away, rather than work towards any form of justice for victims. It also reveals how those in positions of authority – deans, provosts and presidents, alongside Title IX and Affirmative Action officers, and university lawyers – are primarily invested in protecting their institutions. That is the real goal. They are not here to advocate for vulnerable students, staff, or faculty.

Every week, students on campuses throughout the United States – overwhelmingly women – are sexually assaulted. A 2025 Cornell University survey found that 35 percent of undergraduate women respondents had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since enrolling. The problem extends well beyond Cornell: a 2025 Michigan State University survey found that approximately one in five undergraduate women had experienced sexual assault since enrolling.

Yet most incidents go unreported. A US Department of Justice study found that fewer than 5 percent of completed and attempted rapes were reported to police.

Students – and their parents – must understand that the pathways for reporting violations are strategically designed to be difficult to navigate, or outright broken. Although you will hear administrators make all the right noises, they ensure that their publicly-touted systems remain labyrinthine and impossible to access. This army of well-paid administrators – lovely, trustworthy-looking senior faculty and members of staff that welcome you on Parents’ Day and at Alumni functions – answer to the institution, making them unreliable allies of the victim.

Those who are victimised are expected to be the responsible party, documenting what happened to them in detail even as the trauma of the experience is ongoing. They are forced to repeat the particularities of the assault multiple times – to campus policemen and various administrators supposedly there to protect the student. As research shows, being forced to repetitively “perform” for various administrators makes one relive the violation and compounds trauma.

Educational institutions often weaponise incompetence, blaming it on systems that are purposefully nonfunctional in order to avoid dealing with legitimate, even catastrophic, concerns. On top of this, administrators strategically perform care while caroming anyone who reports harm from one office to another. This seemingly absurd game of musical chairs is aimed at exhausting the victims. As feminist scholar Sara Ahmed argues in her 2021 book Complaint!, this process frames the complainant as the problem and dissipates the threat they pose. It ensures that lessons are imprinted on those who dare to voice dissent and demand accountability.

Strategic dysfunction has a purpose: It safeguards the institution and silences victims. The “broken” system encourages victims to keep things in-house, assuring them that institutional processes will be less injurious than reporting a violation to the police. Disciplinary proceedings are kept secret, ostensibly to protect the victims. (Indeed, those traumatised by sexual violence deserve privacy. But these are not the reasons that institutions want to keep things quiet).

Wondering why students, staff, or faculty members who have experienced a violation do not immediately get “lawyered up”? As Dr Sonia Cheruvillil, a public health advocate, noted, “Getting a lawyer is rarely what happens in sexual violence cases anywhere. The vast, overwhelming number of sex crimes are not reported to any authority because they are committed by friends, family. Authorities are not safe. University campuses are a microcosm of a larger eco-system of harm that keeps survivors and victims in place, individualizes their experience, and denies them justice.”

Students may not be able to go to family for support, because not all families are safe. Some are actively discouraged by their families from making formal complaints.

Universities across the US often flaunt their programmes aimed at educating students about sexual assault. They harangue faculty and staff to complete (useless) online “compliance exercises”, supposedly to teach them how to recognise and report gender-based violence. But try to actually report one’s experience of gender-based violence and you’ll likely hear crickets.

As one of my students said, don’t be fooled by those cute flyers declaring campuses as “safe zones”, touting the university’s zero-tolerance policy towards discrimination or assault. They are the public face of the institution and, importantly, part of its strategy.

These are performances, necessary for inaction, for the sleight of hand administrators employ.

And essential to these performances on which educational institutions rely for covering up embedded practices of violence are the women and minoritised people that institutions appoint to prominent positions, meant to safeguard those who are vulnerable to gender-based violence and other forms of discrimination: The Affirmative Action Officer, the Title IX Officer.

As my colleague Rinaldo Walcott, former professor of Africana and American Studies at the University at Buffalo, said, “Title IX administrators – many of whom are women, Black, minoritised people – are often deployed to do policy [work] as well as to do identity-related emotional work. Their identities are necessary, essential. They are in those jobs to calm us down. To make us believe the institution identifies with us and will care. The affective labour of identity recognition that is then betrayed by non-action or other policy claims plainly reveals that not much can be done.”

They are the compromised wingnuts that hold tertiary educational institutions together, protecting them from being held accountable, and deeply imbricated in the creation and continuation of a culture of impunity. Instrumentalising these willing “representative bodies” to be the face of institutions’ public-facing policies is crucial for plausible deniability. Their actual job is to block any efforts to file formal charges or seek accountability or redress.

At Cornell University, colleagues – often those with the least protection and power – are organising teach-ins, sit-in protests, and coordinating efforts alongside their students. Many students still want to believe that institutions can be improved with well-known research focused on reducing harm: “Trauma-informed” approaches. My colleagues, who have firsthand knowledge of institutional violence, know better.

Through their efforts, they are hoping to convey that better communication, even more education about consent, or banning parties at fraternities may not be enough.

Cornell University’s systematic “failure” was, in fact, its success story. Universities have powerful incentives to protect their reputations and keep donor money flowing.

What can be done, given universities’ strategically broken systems?

As my colleagues at Cornell said, institutional processes are “designed to cause trauma, not to offer relief, justice, or reparations”. Let’s focus, instead, on building working counter-systems outside the institutions. If – and only if – we have powerful, independent support systems, and the outcry is significant enough to affect public perception and all-important donor funds, then institutions may do the least possible.

We would do well to understand that universities – and those highly-paid administrators charged with protecting students, faculty, and staff – are also guided by shame and the fear of losing positions and power. Working against what they know will keep you silent – shame, fear, and lack of resources and support systems – is the only way to drag “strategically broken” systems into taking action.

articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv with missiles as Moscow says 808 drones downed in Russian cities
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles in an hourslong nighttime barrage, and the Russian military said Thursday that its air def...
articles.body:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles in an hourslong nighttime barrage, and the Russian military said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted 808 drones fired by Ukraine at Moscow and other cities, in attacks that dampened new hopes of progress in ending the war . At least two people were killed in Ukraine and dozens of others wounded, officials said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday agreed "in principle" to resume three-way negotiations involving officials from Russia, Ukraine and the United States, but no date was set for a meeting. Putin's consent came in talks in St. Petersburg with U.S. President Donald Trump's envoy, Steve Witkoff, who the previous day had met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway.

Representatives of those three countries held three rounds of negotiations early this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva in February.

However, little progress was reported beyond exchanges of prisoners of war, and deadly attacks continued. Russia and Ukraine remain far apart in their terms for stopping the fighting.

Zelenskyy, who says only a meeting of leaders can end the deadlock, commented on the prospect of "technical talks" between delegations: "We'll see what happens this time."

Zelenskyy sees 'no change' in Moscow's attitude

Russia's aerial attacks hit 12 regions of Ukraine overnight, killing at least two people and wounding 34 others, including five children, Zelenskyy said on social media Thursday.

The Ukrainian capital endured a noisy night as 21 ballistic missiles came in three waves, he said, smashing apartment buildings, energy facilities, a railway station and the Kyiv subway system, shopping malls and businesses. One person was killed in Kyiv.

Multiple attacks on the eastern city of Kharkiv and the surrounding area left one person dead and at least 13 wounded, the State Emergency Service said.

Ukrainians are bracing for the winter, as a recent escalation in Russian attacks targets the power grid to deny civilians heat, light and running water during the bitterly cold months. Ukraine says Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for an annual campaign that Ukrainians describe as " weaponizing winter. "

The Russian bombardment showed "there has been no real change in (Moscow's) attitude toward everything that is happening," Zelenskyy said.

The Ukrainian leader has pleaded with Washington to supply more Patriot air defense ammunition that can stop ballistic missiles and to heap more sanctions on Russia that might make Moscow pursue peace.

But Trump has agreed to a deal with Putin to import diesel from Russia and waived heavy sanctions on Moscow, while U.S. officials say Patriot ammunition is in short supply.

Ukrainians chide Trump envoy for flattering Putin

Witkoff, the Trump envoy who met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, was harshly criticized in Ukraine and in the U.S. for praising the Russian leader as a "humanitarian" for ordering the release of a retired American teacher imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.

The five-year anniversary of Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbor comes on Feb. 24. The fighting has resulted in hundreds of thousands of troop casualties on the battlefield and thousands of civilians killed in aerial strikes.

Also, assassination attempts against foes of Putin have been common during his more than two decades in power. Those close to the victims and the few survivors have blamed Russian authorities, but the Kremlin has routinely denied involvement.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "brutal" Russian attacks demonstrated "what Russian 'humanism' truly sounds like."

"Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will," Sybiha said on social media.

Russia says it intercepted more than 800 Ukrainian drones

Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses overnight downed 808 Ukrainian drones, with two people reported wounded.

Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 630 of the drones were fired toward the Russian capital between late Wednesday and early Thursday. Moscow airports temporarily restricted air traffic overnight.

The Russian military hit the facilities involved in making and storing drones and cruise missiles and transport infrastructure in Kyiv in overnight strikes, the Defense Ministry said. Infrastructure in the southern port of Odesa and vessels used for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it said.

articles.title: Meta faces Australian lawsuit over alleged social media harm to children
articles.summary: Class action could be first in Australia to blame social media for harming its users.
articles.body:
Meta and its social media platforms Facebook and Instagram are facing a class action lawsuit in Australia over allegations that addictive design features are harming children and teenagers.

The lawsuit, filed by MinterEllison in the Australian Federal Court, seeks to recover compensation for current and former users of Facebook and Instagram who claim they were exposed to harmful content or developed an addiction to social media as a result of using those platforms, the law firm said in a statement released on Thursday.

“This proceeding raises important questions about the design and operation of social media platforms and their impact on children and teenagers in Australia. Those questions will now be considered through the Federal Court process,” MinterEllison Partner William Nolan said in the statement.

The class action suit was filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs who allege they were harmed by Meta while they were below the age of 18.

In a suppression order on Monday, the court prohibited the reporting of any information that could reveal their identities and the statement of claim.

“We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously,” a Meta spokesperson said.

Litigation Lending Services said it was funding the class action for Australian families who “would have no practical means of pursuing these claims against a global technology giant”.

The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and Big Tech after a world-first ban on social media for children below 16 in 2025, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.

Meta agreed in August to pay $18bn to settle with nearly all US states to resolve claims that it designed social media to addict children.

articles.title: In winter 2022, Emily Ford spent 28 days crossing Minnesota’s million-acre Boundary Waters with her dog; the expedition raised more than $5,000 and highlighted mining concerns
articles.summary: In 2023, Emily Ford undertook a month-long skijoring expedition in Minnesota's Boundary Waters to raise awareness about copper-sulfide mining threats while promoting inclusivity in outdoor activities.
articles.body: The Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness lies along Minnesota’s northern border with Ontario, a region of lakes, portages and forest that draws paddlers from across the country in summer. In winter, the lakes freeze and the canoe trails become snow-packed paths used by fewer people. There has been an ongoing debate about the possible copper-sulfide mining in the area near the wilderness and there have been various attempts by conservationists to keep the issue in the public eye. One such attempt was made by Emily Ford, a thru-hiker from Duluth, Minnesota, who hikes with her sled dog. She chose winter on purpose because most people think of the Boundary Waters in summer.Ford’s Ice Age Trail hike and the Friends of the Boundary Waters sponsorshipFord had already completed Wisconsin’s 1,200-mile Ice Age Trail in winter with her sled dog, Diggins, as the Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness note in the post Emily Ford to Ski Across the Boundary Waters. She was then sponsored by the group in a planned 210-mile winter journey from the westernmost point of the wilderness to Lake Superior in Grand Portage via the border route referred to as the Voyageur’s Highway. There are two listed objectives of the campaign: to raise awareness about copper sulfide mining and to promote diversity and inclusivity in the outdoors.A 28-day expedition from Crane Lake ExplorersWeb reported that the pair would begin their journey from Crane Lake on February 11, 2022, combining skiing, snowshoeing and carrying their supplies on foot. She would pull her pulk with supplies and carry snowshoes for the portages through deep snow. The Friends of the Boundary Waters event page summarizes the journey as a 28-day winter expedition by Ford and her dog. According to Ford, she intended to bring the face of the wilderness into wintertime. The Quetico Superior Foundation article titled “Adventurer Emily Ford faced slush, wind, ice in 200-mile Boundary Waters crossing” is the source for this account of the expedition.Training at Wintergreen Lodge According to the article by the foundation, Ford was trained at Wintergreen Lodge in Ely, an outfit that conducts dog sledding and winter camping. The training was done by Paul and Sue Schurke. Ford had intended to skijor behind Diggins for the whole expedition, but deep snow made that impossible. She said that Diggins is a lead dog that makes its own decisions.Slush, wind, ice and a blizzard, then an early finish on March 11, 2022The article by the foundation notes that the crossing was full of freezing temperatures, slush, wind and ice, with stretches of loneliness. According to Hilleberg, the tent manufacturer, the two experienced blizzard conditions but stayed warm in their tent. The journey ended on March 11, 2022, falling short of the original destination of Grand Portage. The open water on the Pigeon River made them deviate from their route, and the two finished their journey via a ride to Grand Marais.More than $5,000 raised to send young people to the Boundary WatersQuetico Superior Wilderness News reported that Emily Ford raised more than $5,000 during her expedition for Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness to help young people from underserved backgrounds experience the Boundary Waters. In the same article, Communications Director Pete Marshall stated that Ford's story was inspiring. For Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness, the fundraising fits a broader goal of encouraging people to experience the wilderness. The Nelson Institute at UW-Madison notes that the Trump administration restored Twin Metals’ federal mineral leases in 2018.Those leases were canceled in January 2022, one month before Ford left Crane Lake. Less than a year after the expedition ended, on January 26, 2023, Interior Secretary Deb Haaland signed Public Land Order 7917, withdrawing approximately 225,504 acres of land in Minnesota’s Superior National Forest from new mineral and geothermal leasing for 20 years, subject to valid existing rights. Conservation advocates saw the order as an added safeguard for the Boundary Waters watershed, the institute notes.The film A Voice for the Wild and the March 2023 screening in MadisonIn an associated documentary of the journey named “Voice for the Wild,” Ford and Diggins travel through the wild land described by the Nelson Institute as occupying more than a million acres. The film was shown on campus at UW-Madison during March 2023, after which Ford participated in a Q&A session. After the trip, Ford spoke with the Friends and thanked them for giving voice to the Boundary Waters during wintertime.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Beginning in 1925, Minnesota farmer John Christensen spent more than a decade transforming a cellar project into a 14,000-square-foot rock garden of castles, bridges and ponds
articles.summary: Discover the fascinating story of John Christensen, a Minnesota farmer who transformed glacial rocks into a stunning 14,000-square-foot rock garden featuring castles, ponds, and bridges, now beautifully restored and available for public viewing.
articles.body: Albert Lea is a city in Freeborn County in southern Minnesota, an area of farmland where glaciers left behind stones of many sizes and colors. This meant clearing away all the rocks on the farms yearly, which was an undertaking for the farmers. In one case in the Albert Lea community, a farmer found a different use for all these rocks. John Christensen lived outside town with his wife, Sophie. After he stopped farming, he began digging at his home and the site grew into a landscape of castles, ponds and bridges.A retired farmer and a 1925 excavation near Albert LeaChristensen had been farming in Minnesota for 40 years when he cleared many glacial boulders from his land, Raw Vision states and only after retirement did he realize their beauty and usefulness. In 1925, the magazine adds, he began excavating a basement for a vegetable cellar beneath their house. The SPACES Archives entry Itasca Rock Garden (Christensen Rock Garden) tells it differently. Christensen first set out to build the largest structure on the property, a rock and concrete castle big enough for several standing adults, to serve as a root and vegetable cellar.A castle, ponds and bridges across 14,000 square feetThe Kohler Foundation page on John Christensen’s Itasca Rock Garden states that Christensen built a 14,000-square-foot rock garden of castles, ponds, bridges and grottos over a decade or so beginning in 1925. According to Raw Vision, the huge castle had turrets on top of it and 1925 written on its stone structure. Walkways with steps and archways ran around the ponds, while waterfalls, benches and a small castle birdhouse rounded off the project.Roadside America points out that the ponds once held fish and working fountains and Raw Vision adds that lily pads floated in them. The SPACES website describes the same landscape, with rock walls, miniatures, a circular seating area and a second, smaller castle.Rocks and geodes gathered on tripsThe Minnesota Museum of the Mississippi’s Itasca Rock Garden entry states that John Christensen and his wife often collected rocks while traveling, bringing home geodes and unusual specimens to incorporate into the garden and a second page from the same museum, titled Christiansen’s Rock Garden after an alternate spelling of the surname, repeats that detail. Sophie planted the flowerbeds and terraces, Raw Vision adds and her plantings added to the garden’s lush, storybook character.The last work in 1938 The Minnesota Museum of the Mississippi dates the most recent construction in the garden to 1938 and Christensen died in 1939. The SPACES article lists his name and the year 1939 among the garden’s decorations, a date later than the last recorded construction and the article does not say who added it. The museum goes on to state that his widow and later owners continued to maintain the garden and kept it open to the public and a postcard from 1952 shows it in use as a tourist site.Johnson family care from 1954 to 1985Kohler Foundation says that the land was owned by the Johnson family from 1954 to 1985. After the Johnson family’s ownership ended in 1985, the site declined and was eventually foreclosed. Kohler discovered the garden in fall 2019 through descendants of the Johnson family. At the time, the foundation said that the garden was overgrown but the structure could still be seen and that the house was structurally sound.A Kohler restoration was completed in 2022Kohler’s project was finished by 2022. Further gardening followed, including some planting in 2023 and guided tours resumed in 2024. As noted on the Roadside America website, the foundation donated the site to the Freeborn County Historical Society. An appointment is necessary for visiting; the admission fee is quoted at $5 for adults, though one should call to make sure. A Raw Vision article written in summer 2024 describes the restored garden as enchanting its keepers and visitors again almost a century after the first stone was laid, which fits the 99 years between 1925 and 2024.You use AI every day. articles.title: Austrian and Swiss women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
articles.summary: The Swiss government told the BBC that the freed national was on her way back to Switzerland.
articles.body:
Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.

Austrian national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Swiss Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.

No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.

The Austrian and Swiss governments have both confirmed the release of their citizens.

The Swiss government said Abbt was free and on her way back to Switzerland, while Austria said Gretzmacher had been released after "intensive diplomatic efforts".

"We are all very relieved that Eva G. is free again after more than 21 months... For many months, we worked closely, discreetly, and in a spirit of trust with our regional, European, and international partners. These joint efforts have paid off," Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said in a statement.

The Swiss foreign ministry said the country's federal administration officials had met Abbt in Benghazi and she had received medical care.

"She is doing well under the circumstances and is currently on her way back to Switzerland," it added.

Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis thanked those involved in her release, adding that he was "relieved that [she] is free again after more than a year and a half".

The government said it had established a task force - including the foreign affairs department, police and other agencies - after the kidnapping became known.

It added that Switzerland had maintained regular contact with Austria from the outset.

Earlier, Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.

Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.

Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.

Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.

A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.

Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.

It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah.

Under Gaddafi, many ethnic Tuaregs from Mali and Niger were recruited to join armed groups loyal to him in Libya. After he was killed, many went home. Analysts say this has been a major factor in the spread of instability in the Sahel region.

Niger and its neighbours have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State.

The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum.

articles.title: In 2026, Paul Goldstein undertook a 1,000-mile walking challenge across Britain carrying a 9-foot tiger; by mile 826, his fundraiser had raised about £36,000 for tiger conservation
articles.summary: In 2026, wildlife photographer Paul Goldstein undertakes a 1,000-mile journey across Britain with a 9-foot tiger to raise funds for tiger conservation, surpassing £36,000 in donations. Learn about his inspiring adventure and the causes benefiting from this extraordinary effort.
articles.body: In order to earn money for tiger protection, Paul Goldstein, a 63-year-old wildlife photographer and guide from Wimbledon in southwest London, walked 1,000 miles (about 1,600 kilometres) across Britain in the summer of 2026. His fundraising goal was £50,000, but at mile 826, it had surpassed £36,000. On September 12, he finished at Land's End.The cause is bigger than one man’s stamina. Tigers are endangered, with the IUCN Cat Specialist Group estimating the global population (excluding cubs) to be between 3,726 and 5,578 in 2021. This compares with an estimated 100,000 tigers at the beginning of the 20th century. Tigers today live in only eleven countries and have lost more than 93% of their original range.A walk in two partsAccording to the official 2 Legs for 4 website, the route was divided into two 500-mile legs. The first leg ran from Anglesey to Southend-on-Sea from 7 to 28 July, a 22-day period. After a break, the second leg ran from Southend-on-Sea to Land’s End from 20 August to 12 September, a 24-day period. Together, the two date ranges cover 46 calendar days, including four non-walking days, leaving 42 walking days across the two legs. The Cornish press said the split was because Goldstein had already organised a wildlife guide trip to Alaska.Most days were close to marathon length, with hillier sections shortened. Anyone could join for free by registering, and the second leg alone offered 22 route options. The year before, Goldstein covered the equivalent of 25 marathons in 25 days, from Tigerton in Scotland to Tiger Bay in Wales.ITV News London reported that the oversized tiger prop was created by Norfolk-based designer Liz Putland and modelled on one of Goldstein’s photographs of a wild Bengal tigress, taken in 2005. The tiger and Goldstein have finished more than 50 marathons together, including the Everest Marathon in 2022, according to local news in Cornwall.Heat, storms and fellow walkersOrganisers said the first leg concluded in scorching heat. The second delivered wind and rain along the Dorset coast, which Goldstein told a Devon newspaper was the roughest part of the challenge. Even the tiger was damaged in the stormy weather, but Goldstein repaired it with gaffer tape and a zip tie. He ran a half marathon with Simon Reeve, the TV presenter, between Bridport and Beer, and wildlife broadcaster Michaela Strachan was among the walkers on the route. Fundraising was also rising steadily. By the middle of July, organisers said they had gathered more than £13,000 with another £10,000 in matching funding. By the end of August, a news story put the total at £29,000 and by mile 826 it had crossed around £36,000. Local publications report that Goldstein has now raised over £600,000 for conservation over three decades. The money is earmarked for specific projects.Where the money is spentThe funds raised by the completed hike are intended to support two projects through the UK conservation organisation Explorers Against Extinction. The first is Lighting Up Time at Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh in collaboration with the Corbett Foundation. India is home to most of the world’s remaining wild tigers, and villagers near Bandhavgarh live alongside them. Wildlife moves between forest and farmland after dark, and poor lighting can put local residents and forest staff at risk. The project has a separate fundraising target of US$40,000. If that target is met, the Corbett Foundation will install 90 solar-powered lighting units in villages affected by human–wildlife conflict and 20 solar lighting systems in designated forest camps in the reserve’s core zone.The second initiative is a camera trap research project in Bhutan, which local media characterise as documenting alpine habitat shared by tigers and snow leopards. Together, they cover two very distinct elements of conservation: one is protecting people who live beside tigers and the other is discovering where tigers live in the first place. “Tigers don’t need pity; they need action,” Goldstein told a Hampshire newspaper. The walk may be over, but the conservation projects it was designed to support will need backing long after the tiger has been packed up.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2020, Jamie Marais cycled 337 km and climbed 9,000 metres in 36 hours; the ride raised over R400,000 for rhino protection and local families
articles.summary: In an inspiring effort, Jamie Marais cycled 337 km and climbed 9,000 metres in 36 hours, raising over R400,000 to support rhino protection and aid local communities during the COVID-19 pandemic.
articles.body: The money that covertly funds rhino protection was among the first things to vanish when the pandemic devastated South Africa's safari resorts in 2020. With the lodges closed, there were no visitors or levies, which many private reserves use to fund conservation and community projects. In light of this, on August 29 and 30, 2020, South African endurance athlete Jamie Marais rode a mountain bike for 36 hours at Kariega Game Reserve in the Eastern Cape, covering 337 kilometres and climbing 9,000 metres. Over R400,000 was raised by his journey for local residents in need of food and rhino protection.Kariega Game Reserve, the host of the event, said Marais completed the gravel circuit 40 times to make it to the top. His 9,000 metres of ascent is slightly more than Mount Everest’s officially recognised height of 8,848.86 metres, and the reserve says he is the only known person to have pedalled that much vertical gain in a Big Five game reserve in 36 hours. Marais came up with the idea after telephoning Lindy Sutherland, director of the Kariega Foundation, knowing that tourism enterprises were making no money during the lockdowns.36 hours on a single climbThe 337 kilometres over the full 36 hours works out to just over nine kilometres an hour, which seems reasonable until you recall the climbs. Marais reported the incredibly cold circumstances on a dangerous path, with temperatures plunging close to freezing overnight. Jo Oliver, who operates Settlers Drift Lodge on the reserve, said she waited in the dark at the top of the hill on what she called the coldest night of the year, watching him climb yet another rise.He had not intended to finish at 9,000 metres. Marais told BizNews he had been aiming for around 16,000 metres, though he still described the final total as formidable, with elephants and other dangerous wildlife around. In 2016 he reached the summit of Cape Town’s Table Mountain 22 times in 28 hours, a total of more than 16,000 metres, according to The Herald in Gqeberha.Around 100 people helped make the event happen. Volunteers included cycling commentator Phil Liggett, three-time Roof of Africa champion Louwrens Mahoney, Mountain Bike SA editor Paul Ingpen and video director Fergus Clark, while spectators around the world followed live social media broadcasts.Why rhinos need the helpSouth Africa’s Department of Environment, Forestry and Fisheries said 394 rhinos were poached in 2020. It was a 33% drop from 594 in 2019 and the sixth consecutive year of decline. Of those, 247 were killed in national parks, including 245 in Kruger National Park. The department said lockdown restrictions curtailed the movement of alleged poachers and rhino-horn smugglers, contributing to the decline in poaching. It cautioned that poaching increased later in the year as restrictions eased, particularly in December. Its provincial table recorded zero poached rhinos in the Eastern Cape in 2020, down from two the year before. Kariega itself notes that more than 8,000 rhinos were killed in South Africa between 2009 and 2019 and that the country is home to more than 80% of the world’s remaining rhinos.On 2 March 2012, a female rhino and two male rhinos were killed near Kariega. Both bulls perished. The cow lived and became the first rhino known to have survived poaching, the reserve said. Her staff called her Thandi, an isiXhosa word for courage. The reserve has since operated a full-time Anti-Poaching Unit with canine support, tracking and monitoring devices and frequent dehorning, according to the Kariega Foundation.Where the money went That was one of two units that benefited from Marais’ ride. The R400,000 supported both the anti-poaching unit and community food aid, including soup meals run by the foundation. The reserve had been closed for five months at the time of the incident, with its lodges partially reopening to South African guests from 1 September. Foundation trustee Graeme Rushmere said the support from around the world had been overwhelming for the team, and he hoped the ride would motivate others to help those in need through the trials of the pandemic.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fighting rages in Yemen’s Taiz as UN warns nearly 260,000 displaced
articles.summary: Yemen’s government forces launched hundreds of strikes on Houthi locations, a spokesperson says.
articles.body:
Fighting has intensified in Yemen’s Taiz province between forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis, as the United Nations warns that thousands of civilians are being uprooted.

Government forces spokesperson Majid al-Nazili said on Wednesday that they launched 835 targeting operations against the Houthis, known as Ansar Allah, killing or injuring 285 of the armed group’s members and destroying its battle tanks and weapons stores.

He said intense clashes also took place in the strategic highlands of Jabal Han in western Taiz, which overlook areas connecting the province to the Yemeni government’s Aden base. Heavy fighting was reported in the Dhubab and al-Masrakh districts.

A source in the Yemeni government’s military told Al Jazeera that its air raids had struck Houthi gatherings and infrastructure in the Maafar directorate, south of Taiz.

Yemen’s government later threatened to expand attacks to target rallies staged by the Houthis, claiming the group uses those events to recruit children into combat.

In a statement on Thursday, the ministry of defence warned civilians in Houthi-held areas to avoid any Houthi rallies or “cultural courses”, saying the gatherings would be viewed as legitimate military targets.

As fighting rages between the Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthis, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said almost 260,000 people have been displaced since August. About half of them have taken refuge in Taiz, where fighting is now concentrated, the agency said.

In a report released late on Wednesday, OCHA said the UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR) has verified 251 civilian casualties, including 57 people killed and 194 injured. Half of those killed were children.

“Despite extremely difficult conditions,” humanitarian partners have reached more than 174,000 displaced people since August, “nearly six in 10 displaced households,” providing food, hygiene kits and emergency cash in the first days after they were uprooted, OCHA said.

“Newly displaced families say that their most pressing need is shelter, followed by food and cash,” OCHA said.

Yemen’s Ministry of Education earlier announced that more than 2.5 million children are out of school because of the conflict.

The latest reports come as Yemen’s government forces press on with their “Dawn of Yemen” counteroffensive launched earlier this month to recapture Houthi-held areas, including the capital, Sanaa, with support from the Saudi-led coalition.

The operation followed the Houthis’ declaration of a blockade on Saudi Arabia in the crucial Bab al-Mandeb strait in July, as well as lightning offensives that saw the group swiftly seize strategic areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

The Houthis have also launched attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia, striking the kingdom’s airports in what analysts say is a pressure campaign to force a political resolution. Houthi forces say the strikes are in retaliation for Saudi Arabia’s longstanding restrictions on Houthi-controlled airports and seaports, including Sanaa airport.

Saudi Arabia’s Authority of Civil Aviation said on Thursday that the death toll has risen to two following a Houthi strike on the King Fahd airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening.

Meanwhile, the US State Department said on Wednesday that it ordered non-essential staff and family members at its embassy in Riyadh to leave the country, raising fears of further escalation.

The embassy was already badly damaged at the onset of the US-Israel war on Iran and had been operating on a lean rota of staff, although some had recently returned.

In a new travel alert, the State Department warned Americans that “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area”.

In Yemen, government forces accused the Houthis of striking the Aden and al-Rayyan airports on Wednesday. The head of the governing Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad Al-Alimi, condemned the strikes and called on the international community to proscribe the group as a “terrorist” organisation.

Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.

A 2022 UN-brokered truce collapsed in July, as the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.

The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

articles.title: Some New Yorkers back ban on horse-drawn carriages, but drivers fear for incomes
articles.summary: As councillors prepare to banish the vehicles, views in Central Park are divided over the 160-year-old tradition.
articles.body:
After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked.

She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most famous park, pulled by her horse, for six years. But since Lawson heard about the city's vote this week to outlaw the carriages over animal and public-safety concerns, she has been worried.

"What am I supposed to do with my horse?" asked the 28-year-old, who has been driving in the park for six years. "You're going to tell me I can't work with her anymore? How am I supposed to ensure her health?"

Lawson is one of roughly 200 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. Use of the carriages has been an at-times controversial tradition for over 160 years that has become a popular tourist activity.

On Thursday, New York City Council is expected to vote to pass a ban on the carriages that would start in June 2028. The proposal is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who says he will help develop a transition plan for workers in the industry.

But several drivers who spoke to the BBC said they did not want new jobs, and disputed claims their horses are mistreated - even as many New Yorkers and tourists welcomed the ban.

Horse-drawn carriages in New York City expected to be outlawed

"There were a few cases of horses dying in the middle of the park. You can clearly see that they're not taken care of," said New York resident Ron Tsur. "That's not what they're supposed to be doing."

Since 1982, 40 horses working in Central Park have died, according to the Manhattan Borough President's office, which blames issues including overheating and collisions.

New York leaders previously sought a ban, under pressure from animal-rights activists, but faced pushback from city council members and unions representing the workers.

But the ban movement found new momentum this summer after the death of a teenager.

In June, Romanch Mahajan, a tourist visiting New York with his family from India, was in a carriage when the horse bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall out and die. The planned ban - named Romanch's Law after the teen - also follows the death this year of a carriage horse, Deniz, who ate a toxic plant in Central Park.

Several Central Park horse carriage drivers who spoke to the BBC said they were devoted to their horses and that the rides did not pose a safety risk.

Lawson, who was nearby on the day Mahajan fell to his death, called the deadly incident "extremely tragic". But she said if the city was really worried about the safety of the horse-drawn carriages, it would outlaw them immediately - not in two years' time.

The Central Park Conservancy, the non-profit organisation that manages Central Park and supports the carriage ban, said that over the past 13 months alone, there had been seven "horse-related incidents". In May, a driver was taken to the hospital after a spooked horse hit another carriage, causing it to tip over. In January, another horse, named Destiny, ran into traffic near the park, causing a multi-car collision.

Lawson, who owns six horses, pointed out that New York City carriages were the most regulated in the country and said horses enjoyed the stimulation.

"They look at an animal in harness and they see a trap," Lawson said of officials pushing for the ban. "They see a job as something that's terrible. Horses are working animals."

Medet Fidan, a carriage driver for 12 years, feels similarly attached to his horse, calling allegations of mistreatment a joke.

"I spend more time with my horses than my wife and my kids," he said. "They're telling me I'm abusing my horse? No way."

Fidan said he was angry, and that officials were passing a ban without talking in-person to drivers and others in the industry. "If you don't listen to me, how can you come and kill my business, destroy my family's, my livelihood?" he asked.

The city council held a hearing in July, inviting community members, including horse-carriage drivers, to comment.

The legislation to end horse-drawn carriages proposes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counselling, and financial compensation for those in the business.

A spokesperson for Mamdani said his office was involved in planning to find new jobs for these workers - who make around $60,000 (£ 44,000) to $70,000 a year, according to drivers who spoke at the city council hearing.

But the Transport Workers Union, which represents the drivers, said the plan did not include guarantees - including compensation - and that the workers would be "economically wiped out".

The union also raised concerns about a lack of funding for individuals and organisations who eventually take in the horses. It argued that thousands end up at slaughter auctions each year.

The bill forbids selling horses for slaughter or for similar work.

Though carriage drivers say they are committed to the health of their horses, concerns over the animals' well-being have been raised in the city for decades.

The carriages have been opposed by animal-rights groups, including one that was founded in response to New York's industry. In 1866, after Henry Bergh witnessed the brutal beating of a carriage horse, he established the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) to protest horses' treatment and other instances of animal abuse.

People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) and a coalition of organisations supporting the horse-carriage ban also oppose the carriages.

Horses can work up to nine hours a day. They are currently restricted to certain entrances of the park, where they stand and wait with drivers to be hired. Customers pay $72.22 for a 20-minute ride, plus $28.89 for every extra ten minutes.

Vanessa Stolle, a German tourist, said she and her family had horses at home - and that they do not belong in a noisy park pulling passengers.

"To stand the whole day here – it's loud for them and they can't go to the countryside," she said.

A fellow German tourist, Christian Bauers, disagreed. He remembered seeing the horses when he came to Central Park 20 years ago. "It's part of the culture of New York," he said. "Let them stay. It's cute."

Jeanne Collopy is an animal lover from Colorado, where horses run wild, she said. She worries about accidents in the park that have harmed humans and horses.

"I know there's a union and I hate to have people out of work," she said, adding: "It's a little bit confining for the horses."

Her husband, Chris Koenigs, said the animals were "wonderful" to look at. But the death of the teenager this summer was "sickening", and a high price to pay for enjoying the horses, he said.

"The park is magnificent," he added. "I can't help but think, it would be a magnificent park with or without the carriages."

articles.title: MI5 spied on NHS founder Nye Bevan for more than 20 years
articles.summary: He came to its attention in the 1930s when he was considered a left-wing firebrand.
articles.body:
NHS founder Aneurin "Nye" Bevan was spied on by MI5 for more than 20 years, according to newly released files.

Papers given to the National Archives show he first came to the attention of the security service in the 1930s when he was considered a firebrand left-winger linked to prominent communists.

Monitoring continued after Bevan, from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, became a minister in the post-war Labour government when he drove through the creation of the NHS in the face of opposition from doctors.

At one stage the then MI5 director general became so concerned about his links to a Russian spy that he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee in No 10 to warn him.

But some in the service questioned why it was taking an interest in him, given everything he did was in the open.

After his death in 1960, one MI5 officer called the content of the file "remarkably tame".

The papers show MI5 first opened a file on Bevan when he was backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in 1933.

One of the first reports included an account of an anti-Nazi rally in Montreal, Canada, which Bevan addressed in 1934.

"Bevan has inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the Communist cause," it said.

In 1943, Roger Hollis, future director general, summarised what they knew of Bevan's activities.

In 1933 he said the MP had been "in close touch" with Communist Party of Great Britain general secretary Harry Pollitt and party members who backed his plan to organise "workers' freedom groups" to defend against "capitalists".

Although there was nothing in the files to indicate MI5 tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, some wondered why they were watching him at all.

"I do not think that Bevan's activities are a matter in which we, the security service, should be involved," one officer wrote in 1943.

"In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently."

The reporting continued after the war when Bevan was made health minister in Attlee's government.

In 1949 MI5 became increasingly concerned about Bevan's friendship with Wilfred Macartney, "an unsavoury, unscrupulous character" convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.

Recordings of conversations suggested he was passing information obtained by Bevan to Communist Party leader Pollitt.

That May MI5 chief Sir Percy Sillitoe took evidence to Attlee, who dismissed Macartney's claims as a "tissue of lies" but agreed to warn Bevan about him.

One of the final reports dates from 1954 when Bevan, now back in opposition, was invited to meet the Soviet ambassador, Yakov Malik, at London's Polish embassy.

The event "went off very badly", partly because the Russian had difficulty in understanding Bevan's accent, which led to misunderstanding.

"The party broke up in a none too friendly atmosphere," the report said.

The file was not closed until 1975 - 15 years after Bevan died.

articles.title: Americans are making costly grocery mistake even before entering the store, expert warns
articles.summary: Cookbook author Jenn Lueke reveals the top grocery shopping mistake costing Americans money and shares budget meal planning tips to stretch every trip.
articles.body: A grocery shopping mistake that could be costing Americans money starts even before they get to the store, according to cookbook author Jenn Lueke. "The No. 1 biggest mistake is just not taking the time to plan ahead," Lueke, Boston-based author of "Don't Think About Dinner," told Fox News Digital. Making a grocery list and deciding what to cook for the week ahead can help shoppers save money and stress less about meals, she said. SCIENTISTS SAY YOU'VE BEEN THROWING AWAY PERFECTLY GOOD MEAT BECAUSE OF ONE COMMON MISTAKE Another source of overspending may be the pressure to make a different, impressive dinner every night of the week. Social media can offer inspiration but Lueke, known online as Jenn Eats Goood, said home cooks can lean on familiar meals and switch them up with ingredients already in their pantries. CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS IF YOU CAN DRIVE TO MCDONALD'S, YOU CAN COOK HEALTHY MEALS AT HOME "You really can repeat meals," she said, adding that a "base recipe" can also be tweaked seasonally or depending on what is in your freezer at the moment. One example from her cookbook is a one-pot chicken thighs and rice dish. Lueke said cooks can swap in different proteins or add seasonal ingredients such as squash in the fall or asparagus and peas in the spring. NEW PROTEIN RANKING NAMES UNEXPECTED WINNER OVER BEEF, SALMON AND EGGS A bowl-style meal or vegetable frittata can also serve as a flexible starting point for using up any food that is about to go bad, she said. Keeping pantry and freezer staples on hand can give shoppers more options during the week, Lueke also said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER She recommends ingredients such as canned beans, rice, pasta and quinoa, which can be bought in bulk or picked up on sale. Frozen proteins can also help cut down on weekly shopping trips. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ For shoppers trying to stretch a $50 to $75 grocery trip, Lueke suggests bulking meals up with hearty, lower-cost produce such as carrots, onions, potatoes and sweet potatoes, along with proteins like chicken thighs, tofu and chickpeas. She also recommends getting more than one use out of an ingredient. If a recipe calls for only part of a can of artichokes, for example, use the rest in another meal, she said. articles.title: Israeli forces kill disabled man in southern Syria raid, state media says
articles.summary: Civilian with a disability shot dead during raid in Jamla, in western Deraa countryside, SANA reports.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have killed a man with a disability during a raid in Syria’s southern Deraa governorate, Syria’s state news agency SANA reported.

The civilian was shot dead early on Thursday in the village of Jamla in Daraa’s western countryside, where Israeli forces had deployed snipers on rooftops, SANA reported.

The victim’s body was brought to Deraa National Hospital, the agency added.

The Israeli military did not immediately comment on the report.

Since Syria’s longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad was removed in December 2024, the Israeli army has waged hundreds of strikes in the country and routinely moved forces into Syrian territory.

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa has condemned Israel’s “aggressions”, saying they “undermine peace and security”.

In recent days, Israeli forces have reportedly carried out raids and destroyed olive groves in Quneitra province, near Deraa.

In one raid on Thursday, in the village of Turnejeh in the Quneitra countryside, Israeli forces searched homes and detained one person, according to SANA.

Earlier in the week, Israeli forces destroyed trees in a large field by the village of Saida, the agency reported.

Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Sunday condemned “the intensification of incursions by the Israeli occupation” in Quneitra and Deraa.

Israeli officials have repeatedly said they plan to keep troops in what they call a “security zone” in southern Syria.

The two countries have opened negotiations for a security agreement, but the talks have been largely stalled since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.

articles.title: Michigan Senate debate: Key takeaways from El-Sayed, Rogers clash
articles.summary: El-Sayed and Rogers also tackle immigration in Michigan while Kansas candidates spar over Ukraine.
articles.body:
Candidates in two key United States Senate races have faced off in their final debates, less than two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections .

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers exchanged accusations on Wednesday regarding their political views and the US-Israel war on Iran.

In Kansas, Republican Senator Roger Marshall and his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton, disagreed about the rising price of diesel and President Donald Trump’s plan to import Russian fuel.

The results of both elections will influence which party ends up in control of the Senate. The Republicans currently dominate Congress’s upper chamber with 53 of its 100 seats. Democrats hold 45, and two senators are independents who caucus with the Democratic Party.

Here are some of the key takeaways from these debates:

Rogers distances himself from Trump on some topics

Rogers questioned some of Trump’s tariffs, describing them as a “mixed bag”. While he supported taking steps to bring automobile manufacturing back to Michigan from China and Mexico, he questioned the impact of tariffs on Canada.

“I have stepped back and said maybe these Canadian tariffs were not well thought through,” Rogers said, referring to the close ties between the automobile industries of the two countries.

Michigan sits on the Canadian border and is the US state with the most car-manufacturing jobs.

Rogers insisted he would put Michigan’s interests first if elected.

“If it’s good for Michigan, I’m going to be for it. If it’s bad for Michigan, I’m going to be against it,” he said.

He pushed back against El-Sayed’s repeated references to Trump.

“The bingo game ought to be how many times can he put the word Trump in any answer that he has given in the last, whatever, 30 minutes,” he said. “It’s ridiculous.”

El-Sayed accused Rogers of supporting the war on Iran, which he blamed for rising fuel and food prices in the US.

He said he believed Iran had posed a threat to US national security but argued that the 2015 nuclear deal, negotiated under former President Barack Obama, had helped to contain it through diplomacy.

The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) was signed by Iran and several world powers, including the US. It placed restrictions on Iran’s nuclear programme, including strictly limiting uranium enrichment and compelling Iran to submit to international inspections, in exchange for sanctions relief.

Trump withdrew the US from the agreement in 2018, arguing that it failed to adequately address Iran’s nuclear ambitions and ballistic missile programme and support for armed groups in the region.

El-Sayed criticised Trump for abandoning the agreement during his first term and launching a war against Iran during his second.

El-Sayed argued that Americans have been left paying the price.

“The consequences of this war are that you are paying nearly $5 [per gallon, or 3.8 litres] in gas. You’re paying more in groceries because of the price of diesel,” he said.

According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), regular petrol in Michigan averaged $4.44 per gallon on Wednesday, up from $2.92 a year earlier. Diesel prices rose from $3.62 to $6.41 per gallon over the same period.

El-Sayed also sought to tie Rogers to Trump, who is expected to campaign in Michigan on Sunday.

“Donald Trump is on the ballot through Mike Rogers. They are hip-to-hip on this war, and you are paying the cost,” he said.

“Mike Rogers has been promoting this war since before he was in Congress. He’s got a war for everything, and he won’t back off the war now.”

Rogers appealed to Democrats who supported Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed defeated in the Democratic primary.

“If you were a Haley Stevens voter and you came out of this and you said, ‘Man, I just can’t do it. He’s too extreme,’ well, guess what? You’ll have a home with us,” he said, and claimed that a growing number of Democrats are now backing his campaign.

One of the more contentious moments of the debate came when Rogers suggested El-Sayed had the same supporters as groups like Hamas, allegations El-Sayed pushed back against.

“You can grin and you can smile and you can talk real pretty, but I’m going to tell you what, that is a risk to our national security,” Rogers said. He told reporters after the debate that he questions whether El-Sayed could get a security clearance for senators if he’s elected.

El-Sayed called the allegations “shameful”.

El-Sayed and Rogers clash over immigration and ICE

Immigration sparked another heated exchange.

Rogers defended the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, arguing that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations had helped reduce crime.

“We should continue to do that. Find those folks who are committing crimes and get them the heck out of the country,” Rogers said.

El-Sayed criticised ICE’s tactics, accusing Rogers of supporting raids on schools, workplaces and places of worship.

“He supports ICE running through your streets. They don’t have to tell you who they are. They don’t have to tell you why they’re there,” El-Sayed said.

“I believe that we don’t need ICE,” he added.

Marshall blames Ukraine war for high diesel prices

Marshall said Russia’s war on Ukraine rather than the Iran war was responsible for soaring diesel prices during his final debate with his Democratic challenger.

The Republican’s comments echoed Trump’s recent criticism of Ukraine, including his claim that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have caused rising fuel costs.

Trump has agreed a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release stocks of Russian diesel to the US and global markets to ease prices, an idea Marshall greeted with some reservations.

“It doesn’t sound like a great idea,” Marshall said. But he added: “If this brings Russia to the bargaining table and it ends the war, then I am all for it right now.”

Hamilton responded angrily: “What you said just now is you’re going to sell out our friends in Ukraine. That’s not OK.”

Diesel prices have become a key campaign issue in Kansas, where farmers depend heavily on the fuel. According to AAA, diesel averaged $6.32 a gallon this week in the state, compared with $3.62 a year earlier.

Hamilton blamed the price rises on Trump’s war on Iran and called for a temporary suspension of federal fuel taxes. Marshall has also said he wants the war to end soon but has not committed to trying to force Trump to end it.

Hamilton criticised recent ICE raids while Marshall defended Trump’s border policies.

Both candidates expressed cautious support for making E-Verify, a system that allows employers to check whether workers are legally authorised to work in the US, mandatory for businesses.

“I think it’s a good idea. Of course, the devil’s in the details,” Marshall said, arguing that Republicans had secured the border and could now focus on fixing the immigration system.

Hamilton challenged Marshall, who had mentioned delivering babies for undocumented parents during his medical career.

“Did you also call ICE and ask them to be taken away? What did you do with these people?” Hamilton asked.

“You had compassion for them in delivering these children, but then you support quotas. They’re going to have people taken away. Hutchinson, Kansas, I was there. There was a preschool teacher arrested in front of her children,” he added.

Hamilton also criticised recent ICE raids in southwestern Kansas, warning that they were frightening workers and disrupting the agricultural industry.

“People are terrified when ICE shows up because they’ve been militarised, politicised, and so people don’t show up at work,” he said.

“We don’t want people terrified in our communities.”

Hamilton criticised the use of US weapons in Gaza while Marshall defended Washington’s alliance with Israel.

Hamilton said he supported providing Israel with defensive weapons but opposed supplying bombs used in attacks on densely populated areas.

“When you see entire cities flattened in Gaza, now we’re not just talking about rooting out Hamas,” Hamilton said.

“They’re using our aid to buy our weapons and then dropping them on innocent civilians. That’s just not OK. It’s not decent. It’s not who we are as Americans.”

Marshall defended Israel as one of Washington’s closest allies and was asked whether there were circumstances in which he would block a weapons sale.

“I’m sure there is. I’m not sure what it would be,” Marshall said.

Marshall stressed the importance of strong military alliances but said Washington should prioritise domestic concerns.

“I want to make sure that our borders are secure. Let’s take care of things at home first,” he said.

articles.title: Swindon misses out in City of Culture 2029 bid
articles.summary: Leaders of the town said getting longlisted felt like a real win and they would learn for next time.
articles.body:
A town will "have another go" at being crowned UK City of Culture after missing out on being shortlisted for the title in 2029.

Swindon was not selected for the next stage, with Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham revealed as the shortlisted locations .

The town, which was allowed to apply for the title because of the size of its population, lost out on £125,000 from the government and a potential prize fund of £10m.

Gary Sumner, leader of Swindon Borough Council, told BBC Radio Wiltshire the town will "certainly have another go" and that officials "would learn from this" to improve their bid in the future.

Historic canal bank repaired after water vole damage

Girl, 12, gets her own fashion show billboard

Healthcare workers walk out on 24-hour strike

Wrexham, which failed in its City of Culture bid four years ago, made the shortlist this year.

Dr Roderick Hebden, CEO of Swindon Culture Collective CIC, said: "Winning first time is really unusual.

"Generally you have a go at it and you learn from that and you build next time.

"I've been overwhelmed by the amount of positivity. You're always going to get people having a go at Swindon, which you have to ignore - as we know Swindon is an amazing place."

Swindon's City of Culture campaign saw 60 engagement events take place across the town.

As part of the bid, the team was asked to explain how it would use culture as a catalyst to transform the town and the lives of communities.

Sumner added: "You scratch beneath the surface and culture surrounds Swindon."

Hebden said: "We're a bit of a dark horse, no one expected us to bid this time. Getting longlisted felt like a real win and the fact we got close at this first attempt has been absolutely amazing."

The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.

A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years.

articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv with missiles and drones, hours after agreeing to peace talks
articles.summary: Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest U.S. push to end the conflict.
articles.body: Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest U.S. push to end the conflict. Russia said on Wednesday it was ready to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St Petersburg. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November. Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles in three waves. Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards the capital Moscow during the night. The two sides held an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to the Belta state news agency in neighboring Belarus. Such exchanges have accompanied moves toward talks in the past. But while Witkoff spoke of “some degree of momentum” after meeting Zelenskyy and European and NATO officials in Oslo earlier in the week, the Kremlin expressed doubts. “The Americans sensed some new nuances (in Oslo) and told us about this. But these nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said. Russia says it launched the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two, in part to prevent Ukraine from joining NATO. It has repeatedly said it would not end fighting unless Ukraine cedes more land, limits the size of its forces and is permanently barred from forming alliances. Ukraine, which says the invasion was an unprovoked war of conquest, has long dismissed Russia’s conditions as a demand for capitulation that would leave it defenseless against future Russian attacks. Zelenskyy’s meeting with Witkoff was aimed in part at smoothing over a deterioration in relations with Washington this month, after President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and lifted sanctions on Moscow. Kyiv says Washington failed to provide early-warning data on Russian missile launches, throttled the SpaceX satellite system used to guide Ukrainian drones, and withheld missile defense systems bought on its behalf by Europeans. Washington denies any shift in policy to intentionally hamper Ukraine’s forces. Trump has repeatedly rebuked Ukraine for attacking Russian oil refineries while saying little about far deadlier Russian attacks on Ukraine. He called for Zelenskyy to be replaced and said Russia’s actions in Ukraine have been “fine.” Zelenskyy, who long avoided any criticism of the Trump administration, has increasingly pushed back against what he describes as a shift towards sympathy with Moscow. On Thursday Zelenskyy snapped back at Witkoff for saluting Putin as a “humanitarian” during his visit to Russia, when the US envoy thanked Putin for releasing a 74-year-old American captured by Russian forces in Ukraine. “Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening,” Zelenskyy posted on X. “They used 21 missiles. Unfortunately, numerous sites across the city have been hit and damaged.” He said 2 people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in attacks on a dozen Ukrainian regions. Russia said it carried out a “massive strike” overnight on port infrastructure in Ukraine’s Odesa region, as well as on vessels used by the Ukrainian military. In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow by drones launched towards the capital during the night, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added. In the Russian border region of Belgorod, one man was killed and another wounded by Ukrainian drones, local officials said. With the frontlines of the war largely static, both sides have escalated long-range air strikes this year. Russia has particularly targeted the Ukrainian power grid, while Ukraine has aimed at Russian oil refineries. Both have struck data centres, commercial warehouses and Black Sea shipping. The war has ground on for more than 4-1/2 years, defying Trump’s pledge during his 2024 election campaign that he could end it in a day. No breakthrough emerged from three short meetings in Istanbul last year and three rounds of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi and Geneva at the start of this year.

articles.title: Retired Woking decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m
articles.summary: He says he found treasure in his attic where the collection had been stored for 15 years.
articles.body:
A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of Pokémon cards at auction.

The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the cards had any value until he read in his local newspaper about a single card fetching more than £6,000.

His collection, which had been in an attic for 15 years, was auctioned off at Ewbank's on Wednesday for £1.56m.

The Surrey auction house claimed it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever and suggested it could be a European record.

"I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true," said the man, who asked not to be identified.

"When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school.

"I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment.

"He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say."

Pokémon is a Japanese franchise best known for its trading cards, video games and animated television series.

The man said he had bought some complete sets of the cards from someone in Malaysia on eBay.

One set which cost him £300 at the time went for £75,000 at Wednesday's auction.

The cards, all filed into bespoke Pokémon binders while still sealed, were stored in the attic after his son lost interest in the Japanese gaming and film franchise.

Ewbank's said "jaws hit the floor" when the man presented his 42 sets of cards to them.

"When we saw what he had – all in mint condition – we couldn't believe it," said James Spooner, its head of trading cards.

The auction house added the sale had been their most successful in more than 30 years in business.

Its top lot was the Legendary Collection Complete Master Set, including a Charizard card in near-mint condition. It had been pitched at £15,000-£20,000 but bagged £100,000.

Andrew Ewbank, who runs Ewbank's and conducted the sale from the rostrum himself, told bidders he was "going for a lie down" afterwards.

"The build-up to this... has been phenomenal, and on the day it did not disappoint," he added later.

"We had bidders from all over the world.

"The buzz was incredible, especially because the collectors could not believe how good this collection was – extensive, untouched, complete, and with just about every rarity you could hope for."

The record sum for the collection beat the previous best, set only on 9 October in London, when a sale at Stanley Gibbons declared a sale total of £872,000, according to Ewbank's.
