articles.title: Is Neha Bora, India’s new red star, Modi’s real Gen Z threat?
articles.summary: Firebrand student leader has become face of the youth protest movement taking on Modi’s Hindu majoritarian government.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – As India’s leader of the opposition, Rahul Gandhi, marched with tens of thousands of supporters to the country’s Supreme Court on October 12 to submit a petition seeking the sacking of the nation’s election chief, he rested his hands on the shoulders of two women ahead.

One was his 54-year-old younger sister Priyanka, whom Rahul – two years older – has described as his “best friend” and most trusted lieutenant. The other was a 29-year-old student leader who few knew outside college politics until these past few months: Neha Bora.

After 12 years in power, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has recently faced a number of his toughest political challenges, as a Gen Z-led movement first forced him to dump his education minister after a series of examination scandals and is now pressuring him over controversial changes to India’s electoral rolls that have stripped 130 million people of the right to vote.

Yet while the satirical Cockroach group that drove mass protests at Jantar Mantar in the heart of the capital New Delhi over the last few months has grabbed more global headlines, Bora, from a left student group, has rapidly emerged as one of the most defiant faces of a generation that is challenging Modi’s grip on power.

Bora is slight of build, with dark hair, and speaks in a deep, resonant voice. But where Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders have sat in for protests, held placards, and quickly been picked up by police, Bora has made almost a game out of tricking security forces out to get protesters – using street politics tactics that have turned the student into a cult figure among sections of the country’s youth unhappy with Modi’s policies and appointees.

Software developers have turned Bora into video-game characters, leaping over barricades, collecting “democracy” points and dodging police in Mario-style games. Social media users edit and share Bora’s quick-paced fan edits, confronting police personnel, shared by tens of thousands and viewed by millions. And veteran opposition leaders like Gandhi lean on the student leader – literally – in tense situations.

“Can we please, please call Neha the Goddess of Democracy,” asked Nishita Nath, a 24-year-old student in the capital, sitting under a tree in central Delhi earlier this month. The reference was to Hong Kong protest leader Agnes Chow, who earned that epithet as she campaigned against laws that critics have called draconian, imposed by Beijing on the Chinese territory.

Such comparisons, though, are the last thing Bora wants – as a leader of a protest movement seeking to cut a political demigod down to size.

Bora has spent nearly a decade studying the arts at universities in Delhi, including as a postdoctoral theatre student at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), a premier public university that has been a cauldron of political activism for decades.

There, Bora joined the left student organisation, All India Students’ Association (AISA), which has been a major force at JNU for more than three decades.

Now the national president of AISA, Bora and comrades joined the Cockroach activists earlier this year in camping for weeks at Jantar Mantar seeking the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

But it was earlier this month that Bora moved from the sidelines to centre stage in the national consciousness.

On October 10, the Modi government locked down the heart of the capital New Delhi as thousands of young people prepared to protest, demanding the election chief’s resignation.

Police moved swiftly to detain protesters arriving by train and buses, confined student leaders to their homes, and even boarded a plane to detain top leaders of the Cockroach movement moments after the plane landed in the capital.

But Bora disappeared into the shadows, remaining beyond the police’s reach.

Then, that afternoon, Bora appeared live on Instagram, wearing a One Piece T-shirt – a symbol adopted by global Gen Z protest movements – and leading a crowd of a few hundred through affluent South Delhi, kilometres from the police barricades.

In half an hour, the police chased down Bora, who was dragged away in a police van and released many hours later.

To understand Bora’s street politics, one needs to turn a few pages back. The AISA was founded in August 1990 as the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation, a party that emerged from a Maoist-led communist rebellion that began in eastern India in 1967, inspired by a peasant uprising in the village of Naxalbari, West Bengal. The Maoists were called Naxals, after the village.

The party operated clandestinely in the face of state crackdown for at least three decades before rejecting armed violence – a number of its splinters, however, still seek a violent overthrow of the Indian state – and embracing parliamentary democracy in the 1990s.

But the party has changed, although it retains some of its legacy DNA. On October 10, AISA knew that the police would preemptively come after youth leaders. So its activists hid Bora.

“We have been an underground party before, before our party contested elections; so, we followed the same tactics, some kind of guerrilla [tactics],” said Danish Ali, a 25-year-old AISA student leader and a friend of Bora.

Ali said the party relies on tactics that “revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh” – an anti-colonial activist who was executed by British authorities in 1931, aged 23 – “used in resisting colonial rule.”

While Bhagat Singh, a self-described socialist in his time, remains a hero worshipped across political strains, Modi’s Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party has demonised left politics. In parliament and state legislatures, too, left parties have in recent years suffered historic setbacks.

After protests won the resignation of Education Minister Pradhan, the prime minister cautioned in his Independence Day Speech in August against “urban naxals” or “intellectual naxals” – references that Modi’s party have used to describe opponents and critics of all political stripes.

There’s a reason, argues Bora, that Modi’s party is so scared of the left.

“How do you claim to be the champions of nationalism if you do not delegitimise the people who are actual inheritors of the radical legacy that got India independence?” Bora said, speaking to Al Jazeera.

Breaking with her family – and a motherly massage

Bora was born in Khatima, a small town in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand. The family then lived in Jammu, Bengaluru, Amritsar, and Lucknow as her father’s service in the Indian Army frequently took them from one posting to another.

As a teenager, differences in political opinions with the family grew, to a point where Bora was “cut off”. Then, a few months ago, Bora staged a 23-day hunger strike in solidarity with the students at the Jantar Mantar protest strip.

Bora recalled being surprised when someone among the thousands-strong crowd said: “A woman is there, saying she is your mother; shall I let her in?” A motherly leg massage followed.

That hunger strike also helped establish her on a national level, where people could finally engage with her left politics, said N Sai Balaji, a senior AISA leader, who advises Bora closely.

“India’s aspirational class, who felt betrayed by the government’s broken promises, found hope in people like Neha who were sitting selflessly. That’s where the whole propaganda vanishes. Suddenly, the so-called ‘anti-nationals’ become humans too,” Balaji told Al Jazeera, referring to a term often used by Modi government supporters for critics.

The cameras on Bora are new, but the activism and talent for political mobilisation are not.

In 2019, protests against proposed amendments to India’s citizenship laws, which were seen as discriminatory against Muslims, were a true political awakening, Bora told Al Jazeera.

That kickstarted Bora’s participation and eventual leadership of students-led movements. At JNU, Bora “distributed pamphlets and mobilised students for years, canvassing students’ votes for AISA, going to room to room”, Ali said.

Bora lives and breathes politics, “speaking out for Muslim political prisoners”, for instance, he added, referring to youth leaders like Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, who have now been in jail for more than six years without a trial. Bora, he said, is “bravely honest”.

The October 10 episode, when Bora evaded the police, was no one-off. Multiple smaller coups followed that week, as Bora outmanoeuvred government forces to stage demonstrations with supporters in parts of central Delhi.

Then Bora’s photos and videos would flood social media by evening: Straining against the officers’ grip, yet smiling for the cameras, flashing a victory sign, fighting to break free, often hoisted in the air by policewomen.

Bora listens to ghazals by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, the celebrated Pakistani vocalist who brought Sufi music to a global audience.

But the young left leader is a good singer too, say friends, and plays the tambourine.

And unlike many others from that political ideology in previous generations who have been criticised for being too dogmatic and theoretical in their use of Marxism, Bora is the new generation student, Balaji points out, “who grew up on the internet and knows that language [to engage with youth] very well”.

Still, despite Bora’s growing political stature, any left student leader faces a string of formidable challenges to leave a mark in Indian politics, analysts say.

First, AISA’s influence is concentrated in university campuses and pockets of student activism in northern India. Its parent party, the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation, is also a small force in national politics.

The party has two members in parliament, both from the eastern state of Bihar, and has never governed a state on its own.

“AISA does not have a formidable bridge for its student leaders to transition from campus to constituencies,” said Asim Ali, a political analyst based in New Delhi.

In Indian electoral politics, a politician needs a geographical stronghold, Ali argued, where they have a reliable block of voters on the ground. “Bora does not have that kind of blocks or a base,” he added.

One way into electoral politics for leaders like Bora is to transition into a mainstream political party with wider presence in India – such as Gandhi’s Congress party – like many left leaders have done. But there, different challenges exist. “Mere popular appeal doesn’t float you through entrenched hold of existing leaders in big parties like the Congress,” said the analyst.

Nonetheless, whether Bora stays with her left-aligned party or moves closer to groups like the Congress, “Neha appears to be rising above nuances of political cleavages – and building a real block of young voters behind her, even if it is not a textbook voter bank in the Indian context,” Ali, the analyst, said.

Among them is Nath, the Delhi University student who isn’t a member of AISA but is a staunch Bora supporter. She often ends up chasing the student leader on streets amid protests. Last week, Nath spent hours every morning running in her neighbourhood “to practice and keep up with Neha”.

“The way Neha speaks: The pauses, the tune in her voice, the flying hair. All I see on my Instagram is Neha,” Nath said. “My last week’s high point was when I held Neha’s hand while she was running in the chaos.”

That chaos likely isn’t going anywhere, with the Modi government facing pressure from the mainstream opposition, the Cockroach movement, and student groups.

Nor is Bora, says Ali, the political analyst.

Bora “is tapping a newfound place in Indian politics”, he said. “Neha is not a moment, for sure, but is here to stay.”

Milner, Georgia, City Manager Tausha Grose told the city council Monday night that the townâs entire full-time police force and most of its part-time volunteer officers have resigned. Grose also announced her own resignation during the meeting. "It is with my extreme sorrow that our entire full-time police department has resigned, most of our part-time police. He also said he has been falsely accused of having an affair with the city manager. "City Hall every day, it's got a tracker on my truck, it was bought with personal funds and placed on my vehicle without the city council or my supervisor, city administrator knowing it," Bunn said at the meeting. "Here's the thing, still I'm looking for a glimmer of hope to stay in the city. I don't know why. It's because I've devoted my life to Lamar County. 15, 16 years with the sheriff's office and now I'm back here in this county. My dad was here in '74 policing with his police department. I got roots here." ST PAUL POLICE CHIEF SUES MAYOR, ALLEGING SHE CALLED HERSELF A 'MILF,' SEXUALLY HARASSED HIM AND RETALIATED During the meeting, Mayor Craig Timmons acknowledged the concerns and said he hopes the situation can be resolved. Other full-time employees at the police department echoed Bunn's concerns, with Milner Police Captain Craig Walton demanding an investigation into Timmons in his resignation letter. articles.title: ‘No permission needed to hoist national flag’: Neha Bora tells Delhi HC, challenges police notice
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora on Thursday told the Delhi high court that no permission was required to hoist the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora on Thursday told the Delhi high court that no permission was required to hoist the national flag, while challenging a police notice directing her to execute a bond to maintain peace.The Delhi police objected to the maintainability of Bora's petition challenging the notice, which asked her to execute a "peace" bond before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM).The Delhi High Court will pass an order on Friday evening on Neha Bora’s plea challenging a police notice directing her to execute a “peace” bond.Bora on Monday had moved the Delhi High Court challenging a police notice directing her to execute a bond before a Special Executive Magistrate for “keeping peace”.Bora, who has been at the forefront of recent protests against alleged irregularities in the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The notice, issued on October 17 under Section 126 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), directed Bora to appear before the magistrate on October 19 and explain why she should not execute a personal bond of Rs 10,000 with one surety “for keeping peace for a period of enquiry.”Bora was taken into preventive detention on October 16 while on her way to participate in the Cockroach Janata Party's (CJP) ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ march at Central Park in Connaught Place. She was released the following day.In her petition, Bora has argued that the police notice is vague, factually incorrect and unsupported by any material establishing the likelihood of a breach of peace. It also fails to specify the “period, occasion or event in relation to which breach is apprehended”, the plea stated.She had described the proceedings as a “colourable exercise of preventive powers to suppress peaceful dissent, in violation of Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 21 of Constitution”.According to the petition, the police initiated proceedings before the magistrate citing alleged sloganeering at Mandi House on October 16, repeated protests around Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, and alleged attempts to instigate people to join a protest at Connaught Place on the same day.“The impugned notice rests on a prima facie incorrect fact, namely that the petitioner instigated people to participate in the demonstration at Central Park, CP on Oct 16. The petitioner’s call and the incident alleged were different. The petitioner called for a peaceful gathering at Mandi House at 5.00 pm on Oct 16, and it is a matter of record that she was detained from Mandi House,” Bora’s petition said.The development comes after the SEM court at Mandir Marg Police Station ordered the release of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on October 21, after they furnished personal bonds and surety bonds and gave written undertakings to maintain peace.SEM Ritu Raj directed the two activists to furnish personal bonds and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each until the conclusion of the inquiry. The court noted that they had furnished the required bonds and that the sureties had been questioned before their release was ordered."In view of overall facts and circumstances, the respondents are directed to furnish personal bonds and surety bonds in the sum of Rs.50,000 until the conclusion of enquiry," the SEM court ordered.After verifying the sureties prima facie, the court directed their release and issued a warrant to the superintendent of Tihar Jail for compliance.The court also directed the investigating officer to submit a verification report on the sureties at the next hearing. Das, Ranka and their sureties were asked to remain present on the next date of hearing.Emphasising the conditions of their release, the court said, "Needless to mention, the respondents shall appear before this Court on every date of hearing and shall maintain law and order and will not breach peace / public tranquillity of the area and shall strictly adhere to the terms of their bonds and voluntary undertaking given today. The inquiry in the matter shall continue in accordance with law."The matter has been listed for further proceedings on October 23 at 3 pm.During the hearing, Das and Ranka voluntarily submitted written undertakings promising not to breach the peace. They also agreed not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar until the site is denotified in accordance with the law and said any protests they undertake would comply with the law.The court observed that the immediate measures under Section 135(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) to prevent a breach of peace or disturbance of public tranquillity could be adequately ensured through the bonds and written undertakings."Hence, further judicial custody does not appear to be necessary at this stage, particularly after written undertakings before this Court," the court observed.Advocates Abhik Chimni and Abhisht Hela appeared for Das and Ranka.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: The economy and the war in Iran emerged as dominant debate topics in critical races in Michigan, Kansas and Wisconsin.
articles.body: The economy and the war in Iran emerged as dominant debate topics in critical races in Michigan, Kansas and Wisconsin. Data centers are popping up in rural America, but not all communities are on board. And Trump is using flattery to get Putin to the negotiating table. Here’s what to know today. Candidates clash in debates in Michigan, Kansas and Wisconsin Across the country, candidates in tight races met for their final debates of the season in a bid to secure voters’ support with less than two weeks until Election Day: The second and final Michigan Senate debate between Republican Rep. Mike Rogers and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed was far more tame than their first meeting earlier this month. Polls show a neck-and-neck contest to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. El-Sayed sought to tie Rogers to President Donald Trump at every turn while also painting his opponent as a corporate sellout. Rogers has tried to put distance between himself and Trump by calling for an end to the Iran war and for a halt to the trade war with Canada, both of which he initially said he supported. Rogers aimed to tie El-Sayed to Islamist fundamentalist groups, and questioned his trustworthiness. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied any connections to the Muslim Brotherhood, saying questions about his ties “call into question my loyalty to the Constitution.” He cast himself as a someone who would stand up to Trump if elected into Congress. What else El-Sayed and Rogers said about the economy, AI and more. In Kansas, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall defended most of Trump’s agenda, including tariffs and a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, while casting his Democratic competitor, Adam Hamilton, as a socialist. Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who has billed himself as an “independent-minded Democrat,” vowed to not support Sen Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for party leader if he is elected and slammed Marshall for supporting the war in Iran. Hamilton would be the first Democratic senator from Kansas in nearly a century if he’s elected. More from the contentious debate in Kansas. The debate between the candidates for Wisconsin governor — Republican Tom Tiffany and Democrat David Crowley — focused on economic issues. Tiffany, a member of Congress representing a northern Wisconsin district, vowed to undo various tax increases and return surplus money to residents. Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, advocated for a “fair tax system” that would fund education, infrastructure and transportation. With Democratic Gov. Tony Evers retiring, the race between Tiffany and Crowley is the first open governor’s race since 2010. More from the debate for Wisconsin governor. Then, scroll to the end of the page to explore data in other states. More politics news: For subscribers: Phony leaflets and text messages impersonating a trans right group sent to households across Texas have ignited anger and confusion at the start of early voting in the state. For subscribers: The U.S. military has quietly scaled back its troop presence across the Middle East in response to ongoing threats from Iran and Houthi rebels. Rep. Ilhan Omar for the first time described the search of her Washington, D.C., home last week, saying federal agents’ arrival at 6 a.m. caught her and her family off guard. How Big Tech’s data center boom is fracturing rural America Big tech is building big in rural America. Widespread land availability, cheap electricity and abundant water has led AI giants — such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google — to erect data center infrastructure in those areas. But local leaders’ ability to negotiate with developers is key to determine what communities can gain, or risk, from these new centers. An NBC News analysis shows the number of rural data centers could triple if all the under-construction projects and a portion of the planned projects come online. Amazon is behind the largest share of anticipated new data centers, according to the analysis, which also shows that the estimated energy the new centers will consume will more than triple the current capacity. For more than a decade, people living on the northern tip of Morrow and Umatilla counties in Oregon, roughly 150 miles east of Portland, have co-existed with data centers. Residents are split on whether the developments have affected their communities for the better — so much so that at Friday night football games, “you sit in the ‘yes’ data center section or you sit in the ‘no’ data center section,” a cattle rancher and former county commissioner said. The pros and cons of data center development, according to residents. Related coverage: Interactive map: 55 million Americans live within 5 miles of a data center. Find out how close you are. Trump hopes to flatter Putin into negotiating on Ukraine Trump’s recent overtures to Vladimir Putin have become more visible, an apparent effort that experts say is meant to entice the Russian president to the negotiating table to end the war in Ukraine. Even some in his administration are laying on the compliments. Just yesterday, Trump’s lead negotiator, Steve Witkoff, called Putin “a humanitarian” for his release of American teacher Stephen Hubbard. Some Republican lawmakers balked at the remark. At the same time, Trump has stepped up his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — another tool to get Putin to strike a deal, said Robert O’Brien, a national security adviser in Trump’s first term. “There’d be no hope of getting Putin to engage in talks, with the U.S. as a mediator, if he viewed Trump as 100% aligned with Ukraine in this situation,” he said. Another expert said he doesn’t expect the gambit to succeed, especially in the “absence of a clear agenda coming from the White House” and any clear leverage. What other experts think of Trump’s strategy. Staff Pick: Past tensions between Cornell investigators and DA As we continued reporting on Cornell University’s handling of an alleged 2024 fraternity sexual assault, I kept thinking about another case involving the same district attorney: the death of 18-year-old freshman Antonio Tsialas. In 2019, Tsialas disappeared after attending an unauthorized fraternity party and was found dead in a gorge two days later. After obtaining hundreds of pages of police records from the Tsialas investigation, I discovered an interesting pattern: Cornell police repeatedly asked prosecutors for two subpoenas to obtain evidence they believed could help explain what happened, but those requests were initially rejected. The findings took on new significance because the district attorney in that case, who ultimately declined to file charges, is the same one who did not prosecute Jane Doe’s 2024 case. The records don’t establish wrongdoing in either investigation, but they offer a revealing look at how decisions about what evidence to pursue were made at this DA’s office. For Tsialas’ family, who still don’t believe they’ve gotten a full accounting of their son’s death, the renewed controversy has brought back painful questions about accountability at Cornell. — Pilar Melendez, breaking news editor Read All About It A teacher who was shot in the rampage at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school said she played dead after being wounded. “I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else,” Becky Drury said in a statement. “So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.”For subscribers: Apple’s new iPhone Duo is full of fun new features — and some frustrating ones. articles.title: Project aims to protect rare Teesdale arctic-alpine plants
articles.summary: The three year scheme is awarded £65,000 to collect seeds and plant them in the fells.
articles.body:
A project aiming to help protect rare arctic-alpine plants is set to launch.

Teesdale Special Flora Research and Conservation Trust has been given a £65,000 grant for a three-year scheme.

It will see volunteers work with the trust to collect seeds and put them on the fells of Upper Teesdale.

The trust's founder, Dr Margaret Bradshaw, said the group wanted to raise awareness of the fragility of special flora in the area.

"This project is crucial to support the ongoing research and conservation of these rare species," she said.

The trust is also raising £15,000 to help support the project.

The North Pennines National Landscape awarded £65,000 to the trust from the government's Farming in Protected Landscapes programme.

The organisation said Upper Teesdale had an "unusually large number of rare plant species", including the Teesdale Assemblage.

This is a "unique community" of 20 rare and endangered arctic-alpine plants believed to have "survived continuously since shortly after the last glaciation", between 10,000 and 12,000 years ago, a spokesman said.

The programme manager for natural heritage at the North Pennines National Landscape, Sarah Tooze, said: "We are looking forward to working with local farmers on ways to support these fragile species."

articles.title: Blackpool 'chuffed and proud' to make UK City of Culture shortlist
articles.summary: Kate Shane from Blackpool Tourism says the town has "so much to celebrate" and "be proud of".
articles.body:
The leader of Blackpool Council has said she is "just so chuffed for everyone" after the resort was shortlisted in the competition to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029.

Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham are in the running to become the fifth holder of the title , with the eventual winner set to receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities.

Lynn Williams said she was "thrilled, delighted" and "very proud" of the "team effort" to get this far.

"I'm really super-excited about what we do, how we build on this, [and how] we carry forward this momentum," she told BBC Radio Lancashire .

She said Blackpool's bid was "about celebrating that working class history of entertainment".

"Our culture should be for everyone," she said. "And that's what our bid's about."

Kate Shane, managing director at Blackpool Tourism, said it was "fantastic news" to have made the final four.

She said the "key message to us before we submitted the bid was 'celebrate Blackpool, don't try to be something that you're not'.

"Blackpool is a city of culture to us now anyway, we've got so much to celebrate, there's so much we can be proud of," Shane said.

"We've just got to now rally everybody together and work on what we've submitted and make sure that we're on point."

Meanwhile, Chris Webb, MP for Blackpool South, said now becoming overall winner was within reach.

"I'm almost certain we'll walk away with the prize, because no-one can beat Blackpool," he said.

He said the judging panel had "highlighted the good bits and the bits they want us to work on, and now we'll be putting our heads down getting to improve that bid".

He said judges would visit the town for a day before a "final pitch" was made in London.

Sir Phil Redmond, the chair of the UK City of Culture expert advisory panel, said Blackpool made the shortlist because of "the authentic voice of the place".

He said anyone winning the competition was "the start of the journey" to "remind people how great their places actually are".

Adam Knight, chair of Creative Blackpool Development Group, a partnership organisation who look at art and community engagement in the town, said: "We were quietly confident that we'd get down to the final four, and it's brilliant to see that recognised".

He said Blackpool was "a place that people have great fun, great memories of, they keep coming back".

"We want this to be a city of culture not just for Blackpool and the Fylde coast, but for the whole of Lancashire and for the whole of the North West," he added.

The winner, which will succeed Bradford , will be announced later this year. Wrexham was shortlisted last year as well.

The expanded competition now includes cities, large towns, regions and groups of places working together.

articles.title: A London terrace once home to Keira Knightley and Lord Randolph Churchill has been restored over two years; the 4,071-square-foot, three-bedroom duplex is asking £11.5 million
articles.summary: Once home to Lord Randolph Churchill, Lady Myra Sackville and Keira Knightley, this prestigious Hyde Park Gardens residence in London underwent an
articles.body: Once home to Lord Randolph Churchill, Lady Myra Sackville and Keira Knightley, this prestigious Hyde Park Gardens residence in London underwent an extensive restoration over two years. The duplex, on the northern edge of Hyde Park, is now on the market for £11.5 million, according to a listing by Beauchamp Estates. Spanning 4,071 square feet, the residence has three bedrooms and three bathrooms, with access to four acres of private communal gardens reserved exclusively for residents and owners. The gardens can be reached directly from the property’s private terrace via a gated staircase.The building with a famous guest listThe terrace’s past is quite illustrious. Its former residents include several famous names. Winston Churchill’s father, Lord Randolph Churchill, moved into the terrace in the 1880s, as did socialite Lady Myra Sackville, whose life inspired the film White Mischief. Actress Keira Knightley, Queen Noor of Jordan and oil magnate Calouste Gulbenkian were also among the building’s former residents. The listing does not place any of them in this particular duplex; however, their names give an indication of the calibre of people associated with the street.A meticulous two-year restorationThe residence underwent an extensive ‘back-to-brick’ renovation, with a focus on craftsmanship, quality and detail throughout, according to the listing. The results are clearly visible. The ceilings reach about 14 feet, and the principal reception room measures almost 29 by 22 feet, with panelled walls, custom cabinetry and a triptych of French doors opening onto the south-facing terrace. The principal suite has a Juliet balcony and an en-suite bathroom finished in marble, with floor-to-ceiling windows and working shutters. Air conditioning is the one modern concession. The kitchen is equipped with Gaggenau appliances, a walk-in pantry and a separate drinks station. The listing describes the apartment as ‘beautifully restored and impeccably presented’.Another highlight is the private south-facing terrace. ‘A particularly rare feature is the private south-facing terrace, offering wonderful views across Hyde Park together with direct access to approximately four acres of beautifully maintained communal gardens,’ Beauchamp Estates states. The terrace extends for more than 30 feet, accommodates ten people at a dining table and includes a built-in barbecue kitchen. A gated staircase leads from the terrace down into Hyde Park Gardens, roughly four acres of communal green space accessible only to residents and owners. Gravel paths, benches and mature trees separate the garden from the public park beyond.Rosy Khalastchy of Beauchamp Estates St John’s Wood, who has listed the property, calls the residence a ‘hidden gem’. ‘Hyde Park Gardens is truly one of London’s hidden gems, and this home is a jewel. The rare setting and discreet, convenient location make it ideal for those seeking an exceptional central London home. The scale, ceiling heights, private terrace and communal gardens, combined with the standard to which the property has been renovated, rarely come to the market and should be viewed to be fully appreciated,’ the agent told Luxury London.The tenure is a share of freehold, rather than the full freehold. Buyers will want this explained before proceeding further. The asking price is £11.5 million, or about $15.4 million. That is well below the £19.5 million sought for 27 Hyde Park Gate, a Grade II-listed house on a different street a short walk away. The listing describes this property as an ‘extraordinary opportunity to acquire a distinguished home’ in one of London’s most prestigious garden square addresses. This is the ‘very best of prime central London living’, the listing states.The access is another highlight buyers may want to look at. This residence is moments away from Connaught Village, known for its charming independent boutiques, cafés, and restaurants. It is also close to Marylebone and Mayfair, so you will have no difficulty finding world-class dining, shopping, and entertainment. Lancaster Gate and Paddington stations are within easy reach, offering convenient connections throughout London and beyond.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: James Woods finds serenity settling into his life’s ‘second act’ of song-writing, releasing third album
articles.summary: Releasing his third album, James Woods finds new season of life through his songwriting.
articles.body: Behind his countless roles in film and television productions, actor James Woods has experienced his share of "takes" and "wraps" just as endings and new beginnings have occurred in his creative and personal life. Now, during what he's referred to as his lifeâs "second act" after his notorious Hollywood blacklisting and then later the Pacific Palisades fires in January 2025, which still has him and his wife Sara displaced due to their homeâs smoke damage, Woods seems to have settled into a life of songwriting serenity. His third album, "The Killerâs Wife," is what became a concept record released under his own label, Breakheart Music. Created in collaboration with musical artist Bob Wayne and four-time Grammy winner Shooter Jennings, the album draws on Woodsâ early years as an actor on the road. At its heart is a true story that he initially treated as fiction: his past relationship with a young woman and mother whom he later discovered was married to a serial killer. That extraordinary saga inspired both the albumâs title and its featured song. "Iâm not gonna reveal her privacy and her story. I have no way of knowing where she is now or anything, but I heard that she has a fine life, and she carried on, and she overcame this incredible moment in her life. But I always thought about this question. It intrigued me. Why didnât he murder her?" Woods explained to Fox News Digital, describing the inspiration behind the album. "And knowing her, I thought, âThereâs something about her unbelievable purity of spirit that I think was more powerful than his satanic evil.â And considering the state of the world, I thought, well, now weâve got an epic, literally spiritual battle for the survival of the species, really, as a big idea behind the album." COUNTRY HITMAKER REVEALS HOW FAITH CARRIED HIM THROUGH SON'S MURDER â AND TOWARD COMPASSION FOR HIS KILLER Woods describes "The Killerâs Wife" as "a musical parable into the dark heart of evil and the glorious triumph of good." Other songs on the album explore that theme in different ways. "The Hearts of Men" came to Woods as he was reading Matthew 24:12 in the Bible, a passage that speaks of the hardening of human hearts as wickedness spreads. "One in the Chamber," which Woods calls his favorite track, came to him at the last minute and speaks to the need to be prepared for the violent times in which we live. "Bob does it like a beautiful ballad â itâs so pretty â and everybody said, âThis song is so beautiful.â And then you realize what itâs about as youâre singing it, you know, and thatâs what I love about our music and why people are really responding to it," Woods said. "It has just such a unique flavor." A serendipitous encounter at Dan Tanaâs, the iconic West Hollywood restaurant, brought Woods and his wife, Sara, together with Jennings and his wife, Misty Swain. Tana, who died last year, was a close friend of Woods. The two couples were the only diners in the restaurant before the dinner rush, and the chance meeting led not only to an unlikely friendship but also to a remarkable musical journey for everyone involved. Sara has even become Breakheart Musicâs art director, creating all three album covers and every photograph used in the releases. During dinner, Jennings asked Woods whether he had ever considered writing lyrics, telling him to send some along if he ever did. That night, Woods went home and wrote "Misty Morning" in the Notes app on his iPhone in just 20 minutes. Then he heard nothing from Jennings for nearly a month. "I thought and said to Sara, âOh, what an idiot. I just ruined a good friendship.â And then all of a sudden, I got this song back (âMisty Morningâ), which is like one of the most beautiful songs ever. And my whole life changed." Jennings described Woodsâ first album, "Hear the Thunder Crack" released in October 2024, as an "expansive poetic journey" and told Woods that it was, in fact, the actorâs autobiography. FAST-MOVING SANDY FIRE BURNS HUNDREDS OF ACRES IN SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA, FORCING EVACUATIONS IN SIMI VALLEY AREA Wayne later came on board at the suggestion of Jennings, to sing on Woodsâ second album, "Tombstone Opera," which Woods described as a kind of "Sergio Leone revenge tale." The project marked another chapter in his second act, one that continued even after the Palisades fires. Both albums reached the Top 10 on Apple Musicâs country album charts and have sold several thousand physical copies. Like its predecessors, "The Killerâs Wife" was recorded at Hollywoodâs iconic Sunset Sound studio and follows Woodsâ steadfast rule against using Auto-Tune or artificial intelligence. In addition to writing the lyrics, Woods lends his own voice to the songs performed by Wayne, adding spoken-word passages layered throughout the music. "It is unusual to have a spoken part, but in this album, it really serves a lot of the songs," Woods explained. DAVID MARCUS: WOKE 1.0 IS WHY ENTERTAINERS NEEDED OUR SECRET CONSERVATIVE CLUB The record is available on CD and vinyl through jameswoods.com. The vinyl edition, custom-made by Memphis Record Pressing, features translucent colors and sand-like, opaque elements evoking the seaside, along with a bright-red blood splatter representing the places where the serial killerâs victims were buried. "One of my favorite things about working with James Woods is how cinematic his writing is. With âThe Killerâs Wife,â he really found such a unique way to unfold this mini-opera, and paired with Bobâs amazing musical structures, this album explores so much sonic space that we hadnât in the beginning," Jennings said. For Woods, now 79, this musical chapter follows a remarkable acting career that included roles in Oliver Stoneâs "Salvador" (1986), Martin Scorseseâs crime drama "Casino" (1995), and Rob Reinerâs "Ghosts of Mississippi" (1996), among many others. Woods left MIT during his senior year in 1969 to pursue acting. Numerous award nominations and accolades followed. After being effectively sidelined by Hollywood around 2018 because of his outspoken conservative views and public support for Donald Trump, Woods found a new project in the book "American Prometheus," the biography of Robert Oppenheimer. The project eventually became Christopher Nolanâs Oscar-winning film "Oppenheimer," released in 2023, and helped put Woods back on the map as a producer. Although Woods was reportedly advised to remain "invisible" during the filmâs release â he wasnât even invited to the Producers Guild Awards â he eventually discovered something unexpected. What initially felt painful also helped him realize that he no longer cared about the Hollywood world as much as he once had. "Itâs important to understand, I loved being an actor. I loved my years in the film and television industry," he said, recalling roles such as his performance in 1979âs "The Onion Field." Whether based on real events or fictional stories, he explained, such projects often addressed the cultural and political issues of the day. "And at the same time, I understood that my role as an actor was to take another personâs words and directorial concepts, knowing I was there to serve that." "Those masters, not the people, but the story," he clarified. Acting, as he has been quoted as saying, "is now a DEI exercise." Simply put, Woods said he has turned toward "happier things" and spending time with talented musicians, whom he describes as true "magicians" and among the most jubilant people he has ever been around. "I have this observation I made once. I thought, you know, whenever you look at statues anywhere in the world, they usually celebrate one of two kinds of people: warriors and poets. And I thought, you know, if you got a choice to do one or the other, Iâm tired of being a warrior for a cause, getting in the political fray. I want to celebrate art and poetry and music and things I love, and things other people love," he said. "So, I want to talk about happier stuff. I want to talk about the creation of art. And I want to talk about how we create art, because I love what weâve created, and I think the people who are hearing it are loving it â¦ and I want to celebrate it," he continued. articles.title: France’s Emmanuel Macron says ‘illegitimate’ protests will be banned as cities block demonstrations
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that “illegitimate” protests would be banned in the coming days and blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups and vandals for last weekend’s riots and looting.
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that “illegitimate” protests would be banned in the coming days and blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups and vandals for last weekend’s riots and looting. Speaking after a meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, Macron said demonstrations organised by groups such as trade unions would be allowed to go ahead but could be diverted along alternative routes to protect businesses. “Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic,” Macron said. His comments came as authorities across France prepared for fresh protests following some of the country’s worst urban unrest in years. Authorities in multiple cities had already banned protests planned across the country on Thursday. The turmoil in Paris and other French cities has prompted a strong security response. Night curfews have been implemented in some areas of the French capital, as well as in other cities where calm has been restored. Demonstrations planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned, a move seen by some as an infringement on French people’s right to protest. But high school and university student groups say they will continue to mobilize, even though the autumn school break started this week. The Paris police prefecture said the ban was necessary given the risk of street violence that erupted over the weekend, when groups of masked youth clashed with police forces, looted shops and torched cars. The ban in Paris will last until 8 p.m. local time and apply to areas including the Elysée presidential palace, both houses of parliament, and the city’s main train stations. Areas in downtown Paris which were severely hit by the looting are also covered. Thursday’s planned protests were seen as a prelude to Saturday’s big demonstration, when activists from the “yellow vest ” movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, are expected to join. Some of those protests, including marches in Lyon, will also be banned, local authorities said. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a “massive” security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures. Union representatives said their meeting with Lecornu did not result in concrete proposals. They are now focusing on another big day of action scheduled on Nov. 5, and called on private and public sector employees to join. The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of staff. From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, even in smaller towns. High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as complex and unfair. With the government unable to respond to students’ demands, the school demonstrations and blockades have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before next year’s presidential election to choose Macron’s successor.

articles.title: Closing arguments set in trial of man accused of killing UNC student in 2012
articles.summary: Closing arguments are scheduled for Thursday in the trial of a man accused of killing a North Carolina college student 14 years ago.
articles.body: Closing arguments are scheduled for Thursday in the trial of a man accused of killing a North Carolina college student 14 years ago. Faith Hedgepeth was a 19-year-old sophomore at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill when she was beaten to death in her off-campus apartment in September 2012. Miguel Salguero Olivares was arrested nine years later after being pulled over for driving while intoxicated and providing a DNA sample that prosecutors say matched evidence from the crime scene. He has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, rape and burglary charges. Testimony began Oct. 7 following eight days of jury selection. Salguero Olivares did not testify and his attorneys rested their case Wednesday without calling any witnesses. Nearly two dozen witnesses testified for the prosecution, including Hedgepeth’s roommate and other friends, crime scene technicians, state and local law enforcement and a DNA expert. Early testimony focused on Hedgepeth’s life and her last night alive, when she and her roommate returned home from a club around 2 a.m. Karena Rosario testified that she was drunk and sick when Hedgepeth drove them home but later called a friend to pick her up and she went out again, leaving Hedgepeth in the apartment alone. She returned hours later that Sept. 7 to find Hedgepeth’s body. An autopsy showed Hedgepeth suffered extensive skull fractures and cuts to her face and head, and she was also badly beaten on her arms and legs. Prosecutors allege that Salguero Olivares, now 33, was a stranger who killed Hedgepeth in a fit of rage. They said his DNA was found on a rum bottle covered in blood that investigators identified as the weapon in the killing, in Hedgepeth's body and on a note written on a fast-food bag found at the scene. Erin Ermish, a forensic scientist with the state crime lab, testified that she could never say with 100% certainty that a DNA sample came from a particular person. But she said DNA swabbed from Hedgepeth’s body was 170 septillion times more likely to be a mixture of DNA from Hedgepeth and Salguero Olivares than from Hedgepeth and an unknown individual. One septillion is a 1 followed by 24 zeros. Ermish also said the mixture of DNA from the top of the rum bottle was 48.6 tredecillion times more likely to be from Hedgepeth and Salguero Olivares than two unknown, unrelated individuals. One tredecillion is a 1 followed by 42 zeros. In cross-examining witnesses, defense attorneys questioned Rosario’s account of that night, the processing of the crime scene and the reliability of some DNA evidence. They pointed out that police failed to search some areas of the apartment and later lost some possible blood evidence. Several jurors cried after viewing autopsy photos of Hedgepeth, according to local media accounts. Salguero Olivares, meanwhile, cried when prosecutors played video of a jailhouse call between him and a friend who has since died. ___ The story has been updated to correct the spelling of Faith Hedgepeth’s last name on one reference. ___ Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

articles.title: Shark Tank's Barbara Corcoran saw a New York penthouse seven months before it was listed and outbid herself twice; after a nine-month makeover, the 3,100-square-foot home has become her 'beach house on Fifth Avenue'
articles.summary: Some homes make an impression long before they become available to buy.
articles.body: Some homes make an impression long before they become available to buy. For Barbara Corcoran, the real estate entrepreneur and Shark Tank star, a Manhattan penthouse was one such discovery. She first encountered the property decades ago, when she was working as a messenger, and never quite forgot it. Years later, the apartment became her family home. Now, as she moves into a new chapter of city living, another Upper East Side residence has captured her imagination, this time with a sweeping terrace, carefully considered interiors and a nine-month transformation that reflects her personal style.A long-standing fascination with Manhattan real estateAccording to Architectural Digest, Corcoran's latest penthouse caught her attention seven months before it officially entered the market. Determined not to lose the property, she outbid herself twice and even offered to cover the flip tax to secure the deal.The two-bedroom, 3,100-square-foot residence offered a wraparound terrace and expansive views of Central Park and the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Its location and outlook were appealing, but Corcoran's lifestyle required a redesign of the interiors.The move also came with a practical consideration. Earlier in 2025, Corcoran listed her longtime Manhattan duplex after the staircase became increasingly difficult for her husband, Bill Higgins, to navigate, states a report by Realtor.According to Realtor, the previous property attracted an offer within a day of being listed for $12 million. The sale closed in October for $13.5 million, delivering a substantial return on the $10 million she paid for it in 2015. However, after factoring in approximately $2 million spent on renovations, the profit was closer to $1.5 million.A designer who understood her visionThe new penthouse might never have become Corcoran's next home without designer Allegra O. Eifler. As Architectural Digest reports, Corcoran discovered Eifler's work in a magazine feature while travelling on a transatlantic flight. After spending months looking for a designer whose interiors felt welcoming rather than overly formal, she found a sensibility that matched her own.Working alongside Shadow Architect and RCC Cabinetry & Restoration LLC, Eifler completed the ambitious makeover in nine months. The brief was to balance the sophistication expected of an Upper East Side penthouse with the warmth and relaxed character of a coastal retreat.The result is an interior built around personal possessions, antiques, custom seating, patterned wallpapers and carefully layered lighting. Rather than treating the apartment as a showpiece, the design gives each room its own character while maintaining a sense of continuity throughout.Personal touches and playful detailsThe home's interiors reveal Corcoran's affection for spaces that feel lived in. A dark-panelled library displays artwork from her former conference room, complemented by a vintage golden-yellow Scandinavian rug. In the primary bedroom, a pink velvet-lined egg chair fulfils her wish for a swing, creating an intimate retreat within the larger residence.Her collection of bunny figurines has found a home in the powder room, while owl lamps add personality to the living area. The soaring stone entrance hall makes a more dramatic impression with a sculptural Italian bronze spiral chandelier dating to the 1960s.The kitchen, with its contemporary cabinetry and streamlined appliances, offers a functional counterpoint to the antiques and decorative flourishes elsewhere.A garden in the heart of ManhattanBeyond the interiors, the wraparound terrace remains one of the apartment's defining features. Filled with 12 trees, roses and clematis, the outdoor space brings a garden-like atmosphere to the urban setting, with seating areas that invite quiet mornings and relaxed entertaining.For Corcoran, the finished residence represents more than another property acquisition. It is a home shaped around comfort, family and the pleasure of living well. With its intimate rooms, botanical details and expansive city views, the penthouse delivers on the idea of a beach house on Fifth Avenue, a personal retreat high above one of the world's busiest cities.Images Courtesy: istock and Barbara Corcoran websiteYou use AI every day.
